newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Women play by The Rules to find Mr. Right.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Women play by The Rules to find Mr. Right.

text.p: Women across the country in search of Mr. Right have found a new weapon in the game of love -- they're playing by "The Rules."
The best-selling dating guide instructs women to play hard-to-get with men in order to snare them. Be a challenge, not a patsy, it advises.

The book, written by two women who used "The Rules" to land their current husbands, is so popular it has spawned "Rules Girls" support groups across the country, women who are practicing the art of snaring mates by being elusive and mysterious. There is even a Rules newsletter.

"The Rules: Time-Tested Secrets for Capturing the Heart of Mr. Right," is No. 1 on the New York Times bestseller list for advice and how-to books. It lists 35 rules for women to follow when dating, which the authors claim are a sure-fire way to attract and marry a man.

Other experts in the love guide business charge that following "The Rules" could be a big mistake, arguing that courtship is not a game. But Sherrie Schneider, who co-wrote the book with Ellen Fein, defends their work. "It's not game playing. We think it's dating with self-esteem."

She said "The Rules" were meant to be followed in the early stages of a relationship. They simply make a woman a challenge for a man, she said. "Men thrive on challenge ... the whole point of 'The Rules' is not to get dumped or hurt. We only want to date men who really like us."

Among "The Rules": "Only see him once or twice a week. Don't accept a Saturday night date after Wednesday. Don't call him and rarely return his calls. Don't open up too fast. Don't talk to a man first."

Dr Judy Kuriansky, host of the nationally syndicated radio show "Lovephones," says "The Rules' should be ignored. "The biggest mistake people make is playing games. The principle, to me, is to be yourself," Kuriansky said. "If you have an impulse to want to connect with somebody, let them know."

Kuriansky preaches the opposite tactics in her most recent book, "The Complete Idiot's Guide to Dating," published this year by Alpha Books. Her advice: Be yourself, and if you like someone, show it. "There's no sense pretending about it," she said. "It's inauthentic as a person."

The Fein and Schneider book has also raised the ire of men who said they already have a hard enough time figuring women out. "I don't think (the authors) know what they're talking about," 28-year-old finance manager Tim Chin said. "If I want to get serious with someone, playing games is a major turn-off."
Chin conceded that if he spots an attractive woman in a bar and just wants to flirt, elusive behaviour on her part "can be sexy." But if he wants to date someone, that kind of behaviour is a no-no.

Some women said they tried dating tactics similar to "The Rules" and wound up unlucky in love. "I used to play the rules and do things like not call him back," Jennifer Slencak, a 28-year-old marketing manager, said. "But I wound up dating someone who didn't know who I was. Now I just want to get things on the table. I don't have a problem showing someone I like him and that's always much more natural."
Evelyn Pierce, a 36-year-old teacher, said: "All you're doing is asking for trouble if you start a relationship by playing games. You make it more complicated than it has to be."
But Schneider said rather than make dating more complicated, "The Rules" help women find men who truly like them and are willing to work for their affection.
And men, be prepared: she and Fein already are working on "The Rules II," due out next year.
